sourceReview: Psalm 18:16–50 and 2 Samuel 22:20–32 were read for this group. Notes retain Psalm 18:20–24 as a unit and verses 25–26 as one continued sentence, with distinct original wording of the parallel song. Exact Scripture remains in the unchanged fifty-verse snapshot.

verses.title: Keeping the ways
verses.heading: The singer explains the claim made in the previous verse
verses.meaning: The opening For connects this line to the righteousness named in verse 20. The speaker says he has kept the LORD’s ways rather than wickedly departing from his God. Ways describes a direction of conduct and loyalty, not a route identified on a map. The claim should be heard at its full strength within this song of deliverance, without expanding it into a claim that David never did wrong in his life. The verse turns attention toward sustained allegiance rather than a moment of impressive appearance. Readers can consider the direction of their own choices without using the line to judge why someone else remains in distress.
verses.context: Verses 21–23 explain verse 20’s claim, before verse 24 repeats its reward language. Compare 2 Samuel 22:22. The painted traveler and path are imagined symbols, not a biographical incident or a named road supplied by the text.
explore: For I have kept
The word For gives a reason for the preceding claim. Reading this line alone would miss the explanation’s place in the song.
Have not wickedly departed
The contrast concerns turning away from God. It calls attention to loyalty and conduct, not merely outward success.
verses.reflect: What direction are your repeated choices taking you? Where would you like your actions to reflect your commitments more clearly?
verses.alt: A traveler continues along a clear sunlit olive hillside path rather than a rough turning into shade.

verses.title: Instruction kept before me
verses.heading: The LORD’s ways have content, not just a name
verses.meaning: The singer explains that God’s ordinances are before him and His statutes have not been disregarded. The direction described in the previous verse involves attending to instruction, rather than deciding that personal confidence makes guidance unnecessary. Keeping something before oneself suggests an ongoing concern, while not disregarding it concerns a response in conduct. The line does not name a reading schedule, a specific manuscript, or a ceremony. The unmarked scroll in the painting is an editorial symbol of attentiveness. Readers can ask what they keep within view when making decisions and whether those commitments reach beyond good intentions.
verses.context: Another For continues the explanation begun in verse 21. Verse 22 names ordinances and statutes; verse 23 will speak of integrity and restraint. The close parallel in 2 Samuel 22:23 preserves the same instruction-and-response line.
explore: Before me
Instruction is kept within the speaker’s attention. The phrase does not mean God’s guidance can be reduced to a decorative object.
Not disregarded
The concern includes how the speaker responds. The painting’s scroll is symbolic and does not reproduce a particular biblical manuscript.
verses.reflect: What helps you keep a guiding commitment in view when a decision becomes complicated? Where might attention need to become action?
verses.alt: An ordinary person sits thoughtfully with an unmarked open parchment scroll in an olive-shaded stone courtyard.

verses.title: Keeping myself from iniquity
verses.heading: Integrity includes deliberate restraint
verses.meaning: The speaker says he has been blameless before God and kept himself from iniquity. The second part makes the claim active: there are things he has sought not to do, not merely a reputation he hopes others will admire. Before Him places the concern in relation to God rather than public applause. Within this passage, blamelessness is a serious claim of integrity; it need not be enlarged into a declaration of lifelong sinlessness. The cautious traveler in the art is a symbolic response to restraint. Sin is not thereby described as an accidental stumble, and the painting does not reconstruct a scene in David’s life.
verses.contextTitle: The final conduct claim before the summary
verses.context: Verse 23 follows attention to God’s ordinances and precedes verse 24’s repeated righteousness-and-cleanness line. Read all of verses 20–24 together. The same wording appears in 2 Samuel 22:24, within its parallel account.
explore: Before Him
The claim is made in relation to God’s sight and judgment, not simply the approval of an audience.
Kept myself from
Restraint is part of the speaker’s account of conduct. The line does not offer a complete catalogue of his life or identify a particular temptation.
verses.reflect: Where could a deliberate boundary help you act with integrity? What would make that boundary honest and workable rather than only impressive?
verses.alt: A traveler steps carefully away from broken ground onto a secure rocky path beside an olive tree.

verses.title: In His sight
verses.heading: The repeated line closes the passage’s account of conduct
verses.meaning: The singer returns to the righteousness and clean-hands language of verse 20, now explicitly adding in His sight. The repetition gathers the intervening claims about keeping God’s ways, attending to His instruction, and resisting iniquity. The point is not simply that other people thought the singer respectable. He understands the rescue as consistent with God’s just regard for his conduct. This is the song’s testimony, not a universal formula by which readers can calculate another person’s guilt from their circumstances. The ordinary work scene is an imagined symbol of integrity in action, not a stated occupation, payment, or ritual.
verses.contextTitle: The return to verse 20 after its explanation
verses.context: Verse 24 closes the unit begun in verse 20. The parallel 2 Samuel 22:25 has according to my cleanness rather than the Psalm’s cleanness of my hands. Keep each text’s own wording before moving into the direct address of verses 25–26.
explore: So the LORD has repaid me
The opening gathers the preceding explanation. The language should not be separated from the song’s particular rescue testimony.
In His sight
God’s assessment is in view. The illustration adds no visible divine watcher, eyes in the sky, or human judge.
verses.reflect: What difference does integrity make when nobody is watching? How can you examine your own conduct without pretending to know every part of someone else’s story?
verses.alt: An ordinary person carefully arranges simple tools at a courtyard workbench beneath olive shade.

verses.title: Faithful to the faithful
verses.heading: The prayer turns directly toward God
verses.meaning: The singer addresses God as You and describes faithfulness meeting the faithful, and blamelessness meeting the blameless. The direct address draws the previous account of conduct into a wider confession about God’s dealings with people. The verse is not a complete sentence in isolation: the semicolon leads into the pure and crooked contrast in verse 26. Faithfulness here is more than getting a wanted result quickly; the song’s speaker has already described distress and dependence. The human exchange in the painting represents trustworthy conduct symbolically. Neither person represents God, and no such basket exchange is reported by the psalm.
verses.contextTitle: A sentence continued in the next verse
verses.context: Verse 25 follows the summary of the singer’s righteousness and begins a direct-address statement that continues through verse 26. Compare 2 Samuel 22:26–27. Preserve the semicolon and the joined thought instead of treating this page as a complete standalone promise.
explore: You show Yourself faithful
The speaker turns from describing God to addressing Him. The statement confesses the reliability of God’s dealings.
To the blameless
This continues the integrity language of the preceding passage. It is followed by another pair and a contrast in verse 26.
verses.reflect: What does faithfulness look like in a relationship or responsibility entrusted to you? How do you recognize it beyond immediate success?
verses.alt: Two ordinary neighbors exchange a woven basket with respectful, trusting postures beside an olive terrace.

verses.title: Pure, but shrewd toward the crooked
verses.heading: The continued sentence introduces a sharp contrast
verses.meaning: This verse continues the sentence begun in verse 25. To the pure, God shows Himself pure; toward the crooked, He shows Himself shrewd. The contrast does not say that God becomes morally crooked or that readers should answer dishonesty with dishonesty. It portrays God as not being outmaneuvered by a crooked approach. The sentence gives moral weight to how people deal with God, without making human behavior a lever that controls Him. The clear water and twisting branch are selected visual comparisons. The bowl is not a prescribed cleansing rite, and neither object is a physical representation of God.
verses.contextTitle: The other half of the direct-address sentence
verses.context: Read verse 26 with the faithful and blameless pair in verse 25 and the afflicted/haughty contrast in verse 27. The parallel is 2 Samuel 22:27. The lowercase opening and preceding semicolon belong to the source’s continued sentence.
explore: To the pure
This completes the sequence begun in verse 25. The image concerns moral relation, not a promise attached to using clear water.
To the crooked You show Yourself shrewd
The contrasting response resists crookedness. It does not commend deceit or make God a partner in wrongdoing.
verses.reflect: Where could you be tempted to manage appearances instead of acting honestly? What would a more straightforward response require?
verses.alt: Clear water reflects sky in a simple clay bowl beside a sharply twisting fallen branch on olive-grove stones.

verses.title: The afflicted and the haughty
verses.heading: The song widens from one rescued singer to a people
verses.meaning: The speaker confesses that God saves an afflicted people and humbles those with haughty eyes. The focus broadens beyond his own rescue toward a contrast between people in need and those who look down on others. Haughty eyes describe pride, not a physical disability or a particular eye shape. Affliction is not praised as something to cause, and the afflicted are not blamed for needing help. The line challenges self-exaltation while giving the vulnerable a place in the song’s hope. The compassionate human scene is symbolic care; it does not depict God as one of the neighbors or stage anyone’s humiliation.
verses.contextTitle: A broader contrast before the lamp and strength images
verses.context: Verse 27 follows the contrasts of verses 25–26 and leads into renewed personal thanks in verse 28. Compare 2 Samuel 22:28, whose wording about eyes differs from the Psalm. Preserve this verse’s afflicted people and haughty eyes language without blending the two songs.
explore: An afflicted people
The voice widens to a group in need. The line does not imply that their suffering was deserved or should be left unrelieved.
Haughty eyes
The expression points to arrogance and looking down on others. Humbling pride is not permission to shame vulnerable people.
verses.reflect: Whose need might pride make easy to overlook? What would care that preserves their dignity look like in your setting?
verses.alt: Weary neighbors care for an older person in a sheltered olive valley beneath a mist-softened high terrace.
